goals: Distinguish khadar from bhangar and name the crops of alluvial soil

slides.heading: The ground beneath the crops
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a wheat field in Punjab, a cotton field near Akola, a groundnut plot near Anantapur and a cashew orchard in Goa all stand on different soils. Four soil groups cover most of India.

visual.alt: Table of the four main soil groups of India with a region and a crop for each

slides.narration: Namaste! The soil under a wheat field in Punjab is very different from the soil under a cotton field in Maharashtra or a cashew orchard in Goa. India has four main soil groups: alluvial, black, red and laterite. In this part we see how each one forms, where it is found, what it is like, and which crops grow well in it.

slides.heading: What soil is and how it forms
slides.body_md: **Soil** is the thin, loose top layer of the land, made of weathered rock particles, **humus** (decayed plant and animal matter), water and air. It forms very slowly as **parent rock** is broken down by weathering and mixed with organic matter. Its type depends on the **parent rock**, **climate** (rain and temperature), **relief**, **vegetation** and **time**. A vertical section through soil, the **soil profile**, shows layers called horizons.

slides.narration: Soil is the thin, loose layer that covers the land. It is made of tiny pieces of weathered rock mixed with humus, which is decayed plant and animal matter, along with water and air. Soil forms very slowly from the rock beneath it. The kind of soil depends on the parent rock, the climate, the slope of the land, the vegetation and the time it has had to develop.

slides.heading: Alluvial soil: formation and distribution
slides.body_md: **Formation:** deposited by rivers — the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems in the north, and the east-coast rivers in their **deltas**. **Distribution:** the largest soil group, covering roughly two-fifths of India: the Punjab–Haryana plain, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, the Brahmaputra valley, and the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. **Composition:** sand, silt and clay; generally rich in **potash and lime**, but poor in **nitrogen and humus**. Texture is coarse near the foothills and finer (more clayey) down-river and in the deltas.

rows: Northern plains, river deltas, coastal plains
Wheat, rice, sugarcane, jute, pulses, oilseeds

visual.alt: Table of the formation, distribution, composition and crops of alluvial soil

slides.narration: Alluvial soil is laid down by rivers. It covers the great northern plains, from Punjab to West Bengal and the Brahmaputra valley, and the deltas of the east coast rivers. It is the largest soil group in India. It is usually rich in potash and lime but short of nitrogen and humus. Near the hills it is coarse and sandy, and farther downstream it becomes fine and clayey.

slides.heading: Khadar and bhangar
slides.body_md: **Khadar** is **new alluvium** on the low floodplains next to rivers. It is renewed almost every year by floods, is light-coloured, fine and very **fertile**. **Bhangar** is **old alluvium** on the higher river terraces, above the usual flood level. It is darker, more clayey, less fertile and contains lime nodules called **kankar**. Both grow wheat, rice and sugarcane, but khadar needs little manure.

slides.narration: The northern plains have two kinds of alluvium. Khadar is new alluvium on the low ground beside a river. Floods cover it almost every year and leave a fresh layer of fine silt, so it stays very fertile. Bhangar is old alluvium on the higher terraces, above the reach of normal floods. It is older, more clayey and less fertile, and it often contains lumps of lime called kankar.

slides.heading: Black soil (regur)
slides.body_md: **Formation:** weathering of **basalt**, the lava rock of the **Deccan trap**. **Distribution:** Maharashtra, the Malwa plateau of Madhya Pradesh, Saurashtra in Gujarat, and parts of Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. **Characteristics:** fine, **clayey**; holds **moisture** for a long time; becomes **sticky** when wet and develops **deep cracks** when dry, so air reaches deep down and loose soil falls into the cracks ("**self-ploughing**"); rich in lime, iron, magnesia and potash; poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus. **Crops:** **cotton** (hence "black cotton soil"), sugarcane, jowar, wheat, groundnut, tobacco.

visual.alt: Table of the main features of black soil

slides.narration: Black soil, also called regur, formed from the weathering of basalt, the lava rock that covers much of the Deccan plateau. It is common in Maharashtra, the Malwa plateau and Saurashtra. Being very clayey, it holds water for a long time. It turns sticky after rain and cracks deeply in the dry season. Its most famous crop is cotton, which is why it is also called black cotton soil.

slides.heading: Worked example: why cotton thrives on the Malwa plateau
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Farmers on the Malwa plateau grow cotton on black soil, often with little irrigation, though the plateau gets only moderate rain. Give geographical reasons.

**Step 1. Moisture.** The clayey soil holds water from the monsoon for a long time, feeding the deep roots of cotton after the rains end.

**Step 2. Nutrients.** It is rich in lime, potash and magnesia, which cotton needs.

**Step 3. Aeration.** Cracks that open in the dry season let air into the soil and turn it over.

**Step 4. Climate.** Moderate rain and a long, sunny, frost-free season suit the cotton plant.

slides.narration: Why can cotton grow on the Malwa plateau with little irrigation? First, black soil is clayey, so it soaks up monsoon rain and releases it slowly to the deep cotton roots. Second, it is rich in lime, potash and magnesia. Third, the cracks of the dry season let air in. Finally, the long, sunny, frost free season of the plateau suits cotton well.

slides.heading: Red soil
slides.body_md: **Formation:** weathering of old **crystalline and metamorphic rocks** such as granite and gneiss, mostly in areas of low to moderate rainfall. **Colour:** **iron oxide** spread through the soil makes it **red**; where the iron oxide is hydrated, it looks **yellow**. **Distribution:** Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and the Chota Nagpur plateau of Jharkhand. **Characteristics:** light, sandy to loamy, porous; does not hold water well; poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus. **Crops** (with fertilisers and irrigation): millets such as ragi and jowar, groundnut, pulses, tobacco, rice in the lowlands.

visual.alt: Table of the main features of red soil

slides.narration: Red soil formed from the ancient crystalline rocks of the peninsula, such as granite and gneiss, mostly where rainfall is low or moderate. It gets its red colour from iron oxide spread through it, and where that iron oxide holds water it looks yellow. Red soil is light and porous, so it does not hold water well, and it is poor in nitrogen and humus. With fertiliser and irrigation it grows millets, groundnut and pulses.

slides.heading: Laterite soil and leaching
slides.body_md: The name comes from the Latin *later*, "brick". **Formation:** under **high temperature** and **heavy rainfall** with alternate wet and dry seasons. Heavy rain soaks through the soil and **leaches** (washes down) lime and silica, leaving behind oxides of **iron and aluminium**. **Characteristics:** coarse, acidic, poor in nitrogen, lime and humus; it **hardens like brick** when dry and exposed to air. **Distribution:** summits of the Western and Eastern Ghats, Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Odisha hills, Meghalaya. **Crops** (with manure): **cashew**, **tea**, **coffee**, rubber, coconut.

nodes.label: Iron and aluminium oxides left behind
Laterite: acidic, infertile, hardens in air

visual.alt: Flow showing how heavy rain leaches lime and silica and leaves iron and aluminium oxides to form laterite

slides.narration: Laterite forms where it is hot and very wet, with a dry season in between. Heavy rain soaks down through the soil and carries away lime and silica. This washing out is called leaching. What remains is rich in iron and aluminium oxides, but poor in plant food. Laterite becomes hard like brick when it dries in the air. With plenty of manure it grows cashew, tea, coffee and rubber.

slides.heading: Worked example: comparing red and laterite soils
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A student says, "Red soil and laterite are both reddish, so they are the same." Compare them under three heads to correct this.

**Formation.** Red soil comes from the weathering of crystalline rocks in **low to moderate** rain; laterite forms by **leaching** under **heavy** rain and high temperature.

**Texture and fertility.** Red soil is sandy-loamy and porous, low in nitrogen and humus but improves well with fertiliser; laterite is coarse, **acidic** and **very infertile**, and hardens into brick.

**Crops.** Red soil: millets, groundnut, pulses. Laterite: plantation crops such as cashew, tea and coffee on hill slopes.

visual.alt: Table comparing red and laterite soils by rainfall, process, texture, fertility and crops

slides.narration: Red and laterite soils both look reddish, but they differ. Red soil forms from crystalline rock where rain is moderate, while laterite forms where heavy rain leaches the soil. Red soil is sandy and porous and responds well to fertiliser, while laterite is coarse, acidic and very poor, and hardens like brick. Red soil grows millets and groundnut; laterite suits cashew, tea and coffee.

slides.narration: Quick check. Laterite forms where heavy rain leaches away lime and silica.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Alluvial: river-laid; northern plains and deltas; khadar new and fertile, bhangar old with kankar; wheat, rice, sugarcane.
Black (regur): from Deccan basalt; clayey, moisture-retentive, self-ploughing; cotton.
Red: from crystalline rocks; red from iron oxide, yellow when hydrated; porous, low fertility; millets, groundnut.
Laterite: leaching under heavy rain; iron and aluminium oxides; acidic, hardens in air; cashew, tea, coffee.

visual.alt: Summary table giving one key idea for each soil

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Alluvial soil is laid down by rivers; khadar is new and fertile, bhangar is old and holds kankar. Black soil comes from lava, holds moisture and suits cotton. Red soil gets its colour from iron oxide and is light and porous. Laterite forms by leaching under heavy rain and is poor, but grows plantation crops with manure.

slides.heading: When the soil walks away
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a centimetre of fertile topsoil can take hundreds of years to form, yet one violent storm can strip it from a bare slope in an afternoon. Protecting soil is protecting food.

rows: Bare slopes, ravine lands of the Chambal
Dry sandy lands of western Rajasthan

visual.alt: Table of agents of soil erosion and the kinds of place where each is most active

slides.narration: Topsoil forms very slowly, over hundreds of years, but it can be lost in a single storm if the ground is bare. Running water, wind, waves and glaciers can all carry soil away. In India the worst damage is done by running water on slopes and in ravine lands, and by wind in the dry west. In this part we study erosion and the ways to stop it.

slides.heading: Soil erosion and its types
slides.body_md: **Soil erosion** is the removal of the top layer of soil by natural agents, faster than new soil can form. **Sheet erosion:** running water removes a **thin, even layer** of topsoil from a large area; it is hard to notice until the land loses fertility. **Gully erosion:** water running down slopes cuts **deep channels (gullies)**; they widen and join until the land becomes **ravines** — the Chambal valley of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh is a well-known example. **Wind erosion:** strong winds blow away **loose, dry, bare** soil, as in western Rajasthan.

slides.narration: Soil erosion is the removal of topsoil faster than new soil can form. In sheet erosion, rainwater flowing over a slope removes a thin layer evenly from a wide area, so the loss is hard to notice. In gully erosion, water cuts deep channels that grow into ravines, as in the Chambal valley. In wind erosion, strong winds lift loose, dry soil from bare land, as in the Thar region.

slides.heading: Human causes of soil erosion
slides.body_md: **Deforestation:** tree roots bind soil and leaves break the force of rain; cutting forests on hill slopes exposes the soil. **Overgrazing:** too many cattle, sheep and goats eat grass down to the roots and their hooves loosen the soil, as on many Himalayan and Aravalli slopes. **Faulty farming:** ploughing **up and down** slopes, leaving fields bare after harvest, and **shifting cultivation** (jhum) on north-eastern hills. **Other:** mining, quarrying, road building and construction strip the land of its cover.

slides.narration: People speed up erosion in many ways. When forests are cut on slopes, nothing holds the soil or breaks the force of the rain. When too many animals graze, the grass is eaten to its roots and hooves loosen the ground. Ploughing up and down a slope makes channels for water to rush down. Shifting cultivation, mining and building also leave the soil bare.

slides.heading: Worked example: how the Chambal ravines formed
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Explain how large areas along the Chambal river became ravine land unfit for farming.

**Step 1. Soil.** The valley has deep, soft alluvial soil that is easily cut by water.

**Step 2. Rain.** Most rain falls in short, heavy monsoon downpours, so runoff is fast.

**Step 3. Cover.** Natural vegetation was cleared and slopes were overgrazed, leaving the soil bare.

**Step 4. Gullying.** Runoff cut small channels that deepened and joined, eating back into the farmland: **gully erosion** produced **ravines** (badlands).

visual.alt: Flow of three causes joining to produce gullies and then ravines in the Chambal valley

slides.narration: How did the Chambal ravines form? The valley has deep, soft soil that water cuts easily. Monsoon rain comes in short, heavy bursts, so water rushes off the land. Much of the natural cover was cleared or grazed away. The running water cut small channels that grew deeper and wider and joined together, until whole stretches of farmland turned into a maze of ravines.

slides.heading: Why soil conservation matters
slides.body_md: **Soil conservation** means protecting soil from erosion and keeping it fertile. It matters because: soil forms **very slowly** and lost topsoil cannot be replaced in a lifetime; most of India depends on **farming**; eroded soil fills **reservoirs and rivers** with silt, reducing water storage and causing floods; and the loss of fertile land can push farmers into poverty. Methods include **terrace farming**, **contour ploughing**, **strip cropping**, **shelter belts**, **afforestation**, **plugging gullies** with check dams, and **controlled grazing**.

rows: Lost topsoil cannot be replaced quickly

visual.alt: Table of four reasons for soil conservation and an example of each

slides.narration: Why conserve soil? Topsoil forms very slowly, so once it is lost it is gone for generations. Most Indians depend on farming, which depends on soil. Eroded soil ends up as silt in rivers and reservoirs, cutting the water they can store and making floods worse. That is why farmers and governments use terraces, contour ploughing, shelter belts, tree planting and check dams.

slides.heading: Terrace farming and contour ploughing
slides.body_md: **Terrace farming:** a steep slope is cut into a series of **flat steps (terraces)**; each step slows water and holds soil. Suited to **steep hill slopes** — the Himalayas of Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Sikkim, and the north-eastern hills. **Contour ploughing:** ploughing **across** the slope along lines of equal height (contours), so each furrow acts as a small barrier that slows runoff and lets water soak in. Suited to **gentle slopes** such as the uplands of the Chota Nagpur plateau.

slides.narration: On steep hill slopes, farmers cut the land into flat steps called terraces. Water stops on each step instead of rushing down, so the soil stays in place. This is common in the Himalayas and the north east. On gentler slopes, farmers plough across the slope along the contours. Each furrow becomes a little barrier that slows the water and lets it sink in.

slides.heading: Shelter belts, afforestation and other methods
slides.body_md: **Shelter belts:** rows of trees and shrubs planted along field edges at right angles to the prevailing wind; they cut wind speed and trap blowing sand — used in **western Rajasthan**, Haryana and Punjab. **Afforestation:** planting trees on bare slopes and wasteland so roots bind the soil and leaf litter adds humus. **Strip cropping:** strips of grass or a cover crop alternate with strips of the main crop to break the force of wind or water. **Plugging gullies:** check dams and planting in gullies stop them growing (Chambal). **Controlled grazing:** rotation of pastures.

visual.alt: Table matching soil conservation methods to the land they suit and an example region

slides.narration: Other methods suit other lands. Shelter belts are rows of trees planted across the path of the wind; they slow it down and trap sand, which helps farms in western Rajasthan. Afforestation covers bare slopes with trees whose roots grip the soil. Strip cropping alternates a crop with strips of grass. Check dams plug gullies, and controlled grazing lets pastures recover.

slides.narration: This chart shows imagined results of a field trial on a slope. Ploughing up and down the slope lost forty tonnes of soil per hectare in a year. Contour ploughing cut the loss to twenty two tonnes, contour ploughing with grass strips to fourteen, and terracing to only eight. The pattern is clear: the better a method slows running water, the less soil is lost.

slides.heading: Worked example: percentage reduction in soil loss
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Using the illustrative trial, by what percentage does contour ploughing with strip cropping reduce soil loss compared with up-and-down ploughing?

**Step 1.** Reduction $= 40 - 14 = 26$ t per hectare.

**Step 2.** Percentage $= \frac{26}{40} \times 100 = 65$%.

**Step 3. Interpret.** Combining contour furrows with grass strips removes about two-thirds of the loss; only terracing does better.

visual.alt: Table of the up-and-down and strip-cropping plots with the reduction

slides.narration: Let us work out the saving from contour ploughing with grass strips. Subtract its loss of fourteen tonnes from the forty tonnes lost by up and down ploughing to get a saving of twenty six tonnes. Divide by forty and multiply by one hundred. The answer is sixty five per cent. So this method keeps nearly two thirds of the soil that would otherwise be lost.

sections.heading: 1. Alluvial soil
sections.body_md:
- **Formation:** deposited by rivers (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra systems; east-coast deltas).
- **Distribution:** largest soil group (roughly two-fifths of India) — Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Assam valley; deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri; coastal plains.
- **Composition:** sand, silt, clay; generally rich in potash and lime, poor in nitrogen and humus; coarse near the foothills, finer downstream.
- **Khadar:** new alluvium on low floodplains, renewed by floods, light-coloured, very fertile.
- **Bhangar:** old alluvium on higher terraces above flood level, more clayey, less fertile, contains **kankar**.
- **Crops:** wheat, rice, sugarcane, jute (deltas), pulses, oilseeds.

key_terms.definition_md: New alluvium on the low floodplains of rivers, renewed by floods almost every year.
Old alluvium on higher river terraces, above normal flood level, often containing kankar.
Nodules (lumps) of lime found in bhangar soil.

visual.alt: Table comparing khadar and bhangar

sections.heading: 2. Black soil (regur)
sections.body_md:
- **Formation:** weathering of basalt (Deccan trap lava).
- **Distribution:** Maharashtra, Malwa plateau (Madhya Pradesh), Saurashtra (Gujarat), parts of Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh.
- **Characteristics:** fine, clayey; retains moisture; sticky when wet; deep cracks when dry (self-ploughing); rich in lime, iron, magnesia, potash; poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus.
- **Crops:** cotton (black cotton soil), sugarcane, jowar, wheat, groundnut, tobacco.

key_terms.definition_md: Another name for the black soil of the Deccan plateau.
The turning over of black soil as loose soil falls into the deep cracks that open in the dry season.

visual.alt: Table of black-soil properties and their effects

sections.heading: 3. Red soil
sections.body_md:
- **Formation:** weathering of old crystalline and metamorphic rocks (granite, gneiss) in low to moderate rainfall.
- **Colour:** red from iron oxide spread through the soil; yellow where the oxide is hydrated.
- **Distribution:** Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Chota Nagpur (Jharkhand).
- **Characteristics:** sandy to loamy, porous, light; low water retention; poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus.
- **Crops (with fertilisers, irrigation):** ragi, jowar, groundnut, pulses, tobacco; rice in lowlands.

key_terms.definition_md: The compound that gives red soil its colour; it looks yellow when hydrated.

visual.alt: Table summarising red soil

sections.heading: 4. Laterite soil
sections.body_md:
- **Formation:** high temperature and heavy rain with alternate wet and dry seasons; **leaching** removes lime and silica, leaving oxides of iron and aluminium. (Latin *later* = brick.)
- **Distribution:** summits of the Western and Eastern Ghats, Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Odisha hills, Meghalaya.
- **Characteristics:** coarse, acidic, infertile; poor in nitrogen, lime, humus; hardens in air (used as building bricks).
- **Crops (with manure):** cashew, tea, coffee, rubber, coconut.

| Head | Red | Laterite |
|---|---|---|
| Rainfall | Low to moderate | Heavy |
| Process | Weathering | Leaching |
| Fertility | Low | Very low, acidic |
| Crops | Millets, groundnut | Cashew, tea, coffee |

key_terms.definition_md: The washing down of soluble minerals such as lime and silica by water percolating through soil.

sections.heading: 5. Soil erosion
sections.body_md:
- **Soil erosion:** removal of topsoil by natural agents faster than new soil forms.
- **Agents:** running water, wind, waves, glaciers.
- **Sheet erosion:** thin, even layer removed from a wide area by running water.
- **Gully erosion:** deep channels cut by running water; badly gullied land becomes **ravines** (Chambal valley).
- **Wind erosion:** dry, loose, bare soil blown away (western Rajasthan).
- **Human causes:** deforestation, overgrazing, ploughing up and down slopes, shifting cultivation, mining and construction.

key_terms.definition_md: The removal of the top layer of soil by water, wind or other agents faster than it can form.
Land cut up by deep, joined gullies, unfit for farming.

visual.alt: Table of types of erosion with agent and example area

sections.heading: 6. Soil conservation
sections.body_md:
- **Meaning:** protecting soil from erosion and maintaining its fertility.
- **Importance:** soil forms slowly; agriculture depends on it; eroded silt fills reservoirs and worsens floods; loss of land hurts livelihoods.
- **Terrace farming:** flat steps on **steep slopes** (Himalayas, north-east).
- **Contour ploughing:** furrows across the slope on **gentle slopes**.
- **Strip cropping:** alternate strips of crops and grass.
- **Shelter belts:** rows of trees across the wind in **dry, windy plains** (western Rajasthan).
- **Afforestation:** trees on bare slopes and wasteland.
- **Plugging gullies:** check dams and planting in gullied land (Chambal).
- **Controlled grazing:** pasture rotation.

key_terms.definition_md: Rows of trees planted across the path of the wind to slow it and protect fields from wind erosion.
Ploughing across a slope along lines of equal height so that furrows hold back running water.

- Calling bhangar new alluvium, or saying khadar contains kankar.

questions.stem_md: Alluvial soil near the Himalayan foothills in Uttarakhand is coarse and pebbly, while the soil of the Sundarbans delta is fine and clayey. The best explanation is that:

the foothill soil has been leached by heavy rain into laterite
wind has blown sand from the Thar onto the foothills
rivers drop coarse material first where they leave the hills and carry only fine silt and clay to the delta

questions.stem_md: A farmer near Kanpur owns one plot on the low floodplain of the Ganga and another on higher ground some kilometres from the river. State two ways in which the soils of the two plots are likely to differ.

questions.stem_md: Explain how alluvial soil is formed, and why it is coarse near the Himalayan foothills but fine and clayey in the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta.

answer.model_answer_md: Rivers wear down the mountains and carry the eroded material to the plains, where it settles in layers as alluvium. Where a river leaves the hills its speed falls sharply, so the heavy, coarse particles such as pebbles and sand are dropped first. Only the lightest silt and clay travel all the way and settle in the slow water of the delta.

questions.solution_md: Deposition by rivers; sorting by speed: coarse near the hills, fine in the delta.

questions.stem_md: The black soil of the Deccan has formed from the weathering of ___, a volcanic rock.
questions.solution_md: **Basalt** (Deccan trap lava).

questions.stem_md: Name the soil formed by the weathering of lava rocks on the Deccan plateau.
questions.solution_md: Black soil.

questions.stem_md: Give two geographical reasons why cotton is widely grown on the black soils of Saurashtra and Vidarbha.

answer.model_answer_md: Black soil is clayey and retains moisture for a long time, so cotton can mature on stored monsoon water with little irrigation. It is rich in lime, potash and magnesia, which the cotton plant needs, and the cracks of the dry season aerate the soil.

questions.solution_md: Moisture retention; nutrients (and aeration).

questions.stem_md: Laterite soil forms where:

options.text_md: high temperature and heavy rain leach away lime and silica, leaving iron and aluminium oxides
rivers deposit fresh silt every year
basalt lava weathers in a semi-arid climate
wind deposits fine sand in a desert

questions.solution_md: Laterite is the product of intense leaching — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A soil on the Chota Nagpur plateau is reddish in a dry pit wall but looks yellowish in a waterlogged hollow nearby. This is because:

options.text_md: the yellow soil is alluvium brought by floods
water removes all the iron from the soil at once
the iron oxide in red soil looks yellow when it is hydrated
the waterlogged soil has formed from basalt

questions.solution_md: Hydrated iron oxide is yellow — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In parts of coastal Karnataka and Goa, blocks are cut from the soil, left to dry and used to build house walls because they become hard in air. The soil is:

options.text_md: khadar
laterite
black soil
desert soil

questions.solution_md: Laterite (from the Latin for brick) hardens on exposure — option (b).

questions.stem_md: With fertilisers and irrigation, the red soils of interior Tamil Nadu and Karnataka are mainly used to grow:

options.text_md: millets such as ragi, groundnut and pulses
jute and mesta
tea and rubber
saffron and apples

questions.solution_md: Option (a).

questions.stem_md: A planter on the laterite slopes of the Western Ghats in Kerala adds plenty of manure before planting. Which crop group is he most likely to grow?

options.text_md: Wheat and gram
Cotton and jowar
Tea, coffee, rubber or cashew
Jute and mesta

questions.solution_md: Manured laterite on wet hill slopes suits plantation crops — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Blocks of laterite are used as building bricks in parts of Kerala.

**Reason (R):** Laterite is rich in nitrogen and humus.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true (laterite hardens in air); R is false: laterite is poor in nitrogen and humus — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Red soil is rich in humus and nitrogen and needs no fertiliser.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False: red soil is poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus and needs fertilisers.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Laterite soil develops where rainfall is low and temperatures are low.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False: it develops under high temperature and heavy rain.

questions.stem_md: The washing down of lime and silica by heavy rain percolating through the soil is called ___.
questions.solution_md: **Leaching**.

questions.stem_md: Name one crop grown on laterite soil in Goa or coastal Karnataka.
questions.solution_md: Cashew.

questions.stem_md: Why is red soil red? Why does it sometimes look yellow?

answer.model_answer_md: It is red because iron oxide, released from the weathered crystalline rocks, is spread through the soil. Where that iron oxide is hydrated, as in moist or waterlogged places, the soil looks yellow.

questions.solution_md: Iron oxide; hydration makes it yellow.

questions.stem_md: What is leaching? How does it make laterite soil infertile?

answer.model_answer_md: Leaching is the washing down of soluble minerals by rainwater soaking through the soil. Under very heavy rain it carries away lime, silica and plant nutrients, leaving mostly iron and aluminium oxides, so laterite becomes acidic and poor.

questions.solution_md: Definition; removal of nutrients leaves oxides.

questions.stem_md: Compare red soil and laterite soil under three heads: conditions of formation, fertility and crops grown.

answer.model_answer_md: Formation: red soil forms by the weathering of crystalline rocks such as granite where rain is low to moderate; laterite forms by intense leaching under heavy rain and high temperature. Fertility: red soil is low in nitrogen and humus but responds to fertiliser; laterite is acidic and very poor. Crops: red soil grows millets, groundnut and pulses; laterite grows cashew, tea, coffee and rubber when manured.

questions.solution_md: Formation; fertility; crops.

questions.stem_md: After a season of heavy storms, a farmer on a gentle slope in Jharkhand notices that the dark topsoil has thinned evenly across the whole field, though no channels have formed. This is:

options.text_md: gully erosion
wind erosion
leaching
sheet erosion

questions.solution_md: An even loss of a thin layer over a wide area is sheet erosion — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On farms near Jaisalmer, loose dry soil is lifted and carried away during the dusty months of May and June. The main agent of erosion here is:

options.text_md: running water
glaciers
sea waves
wind

questions.solution_md: Dry, bare sandy land in strong winds suffers wind erosion — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On a hillside in the Aravallis, herds of goats graze until no grass is left. In the next monsoon, soil loss from the slope rises sharply because:

options.text_md: the grass cover that bound the soil and slowed runoff has been removed
goats add too much manure to the soil
grazing makes the slope less steep
grazing increases the humus in the soil

questions.solution_md: Overgrazing exposes the soil to rain and runoff — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Shifting cultivation (jhum) on the hills of north-east India increases soil erosion mainly because:

options.text_md: every slope is cut into terraces
forest is cleared and burnt, leaving the slopes bare to heavy rain
it adds kankar to the soil
shelter belts are planted across the wind

questions.solution_md: Clearing the forest exposes steep slopes — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Gully erosion has made large areas of the Chambal valley unfit for farming.

**Reason (R):** The Chambal is a tributary of the Yamuna.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the river’s being a tributary does not explain the gullying (soft soil, heavy downpours and bare slopes do) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Running water cutting deep channels into soft soil, as in the Chambal valley, is called ___ erosion.
questions.solution_md: **Gully** erosion.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which human activities have increased soil erosion on the slopes of the Shivalik hills.

answer.model_answer_md: Forests have been cut for timber, fuel and farmland, removing the roots that hold the soil and the canopy that breaks the rain. Overgrazing by goats and cattle strips the grass and loosens the soil with their hooves, so runoff carries the soil away.

questions.solution_md: Deforestation; overgrazing.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between sheet erosion and gully erosion.

answer.model_answer_md: In sheet erosion, running water removes a thin, even layer of topsoil over a wide area, so the loss is hardly noticed. In gully erosion, running water cuts deep channels that widen and join into ravines, as along the Chambal.

questions.solution_md: Thin even layer versus deep channels.

questions.stem_md: A hill village in Uttarakhand has cleared its oak forest for fuel, keeps large herds of goats and ploughs its terraced slopes up and down after the terrace walls collapsed. Explain three ways in which these practices increase soil erosion.

answer.model_answer_md: Clearing the oak forest removes the roots that bound the soil and the leaf cover that softened the rain, so rain strikes bare ground. Large goat herds eat the grass to its roots and loosen the soil with their hooves. Ploughing straight up and down the slope makes channels along which runoff rushes, carrying topsoil away.

questions.solution_md: Deforestation; overgrazing; faulty ploughing.

questions.stem_md: Contour ploughing reduces soil erosion on a gentle slope because:

options.text_md: furrows running down the slope drain water away faster
it removes the topsoil before the rains
furrows running across the slope hold back water and let it soak in
it turns the slope into flat steps with stone walls

questions.solution_md: Each furrow along a contour acts as a small barrier — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which pairing of area and soil conservation method is most suitable?

options.text_md: Sand-blown fields of western Rajasthan — terrace farming
Flat plain of Punjab — check dams in ravines
Steep slopes of Sikkim — terrace farming
Chambal ravines — shelter belts against wind

questions.solution_md: Terraces suit steep slopes; shelter belts suit windy dry plains; check dams suit gullies — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A farmer near Bikaner plants rows of khejri and other hardy trees along the western edge of her fields. These rows mainly:

options.text_md: reduce wind speed and trap blowing sand
carry irrigation water to the crops
cut the land into terraces
add kankar to the soil

questions.solution_md: They act as a shelter belt — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In an illustrative field trial on a slope, soil lost in tonnes per hectare per year was: ploughing up and down the slope 40; contour ploughing 22; contour ploughing with strip cropping 14; terraced field 8. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text_md: Methods that slow running water on the slope reduce soil loss the most
Ploughing up and down the slope protects the soil best
Strip cropping protects the soil better than terracing
All the methods lose about the same amount of soil

questions.solution_md: Loss falls from 40 to 8 t as the method slows runoff more — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Shelter belts are mainly used to check gully erosion on steep hill slopes.

**Reason (R):** Rows of trees reduce the speed of the wind near the ground.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: shelter belts protect windy dry plains from wind erosion; R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Afforestation helps to check soil erosion because tree roots bind the soil and fallen leaves add humus.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A steep, bare slope in Meghalaya ploughed up and down will usually lose less soil than the same slope cut into terraces.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False: terraces slow runoff and hold the soil, so the terraced slope loses far less.

questions.stem_md: Cutting a steep hill slope into a series of flat steps for growing crops is called ___ farming.
questions.solution_md: **Terrace** farming.

questions.stem_md: Match each soil conservation method in Column A with the area where it is most useful in Column B.

options.text_md: Terrace farming
Contour ploughing
Shelter belts
Check dams

match_right.text_md: Gentle slopes of the Chota Nagpur uplands
Gullied land of the Chambal valley

questions.solution_md: Terrace farming → steep slopes; contour ploughing → gentle slopes; shelter belts → windy dry fields; check dams → gullies.

questions.stem_md: Match each soil in Column A with a crop it is well known for in Column B.

options.text_md: Alluvial soil
Black soil
Red soil
Laterite soil

questions.solution_md: Alluvial → wheat, sugarcane; black → cotton; red → ragi, groundnut; laterite → cashew.

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons why soil conservation is important for India.

answer.model_answer_md: Topsoil forms extremely slowly, so soil that is lost cannot be replaced within a human lifetime. A very large part of India’s people depend on farming, which needs fertile soil, so erosion lowers yields and incomes. Eroded soil ends up as silt in rivers and reservoirs, reducing the water they store and making floods worse.

questions.solution_md: Slow formation; dependence on farming; siltation and floods.

questions.stem_md: Why is terrace farming widely practised on the hill slopes of Sikkim but not needed in the Punjab plain?

answer.model_answer_md: On the steep slopes of Sikkim, heavy rain would wash the soil downhill; level terraces slow the water, hold the soil and create flat land for crops. The Punjab plain is almost flat, so runoff is slow, slope erosion is slight and fields are already level.

questions.solution_md: Steep slopes need terraces; flat plains do not.

marking_scheme.step: Sikkim: steep slopes, terraces hold soil

questions.stem_md: In an illustrative field trial, a plot ploughed up and down a slope lost 40 tonnes of soil per hectare in a year, and a plot with contour ploughing lost 22 tonnes. By what percentage did contour ploughing reduce the soil loss?
questions.solution_md: Reduction $= 40 - 22 = 18$ t per hectare; percentage $= \frac{18}{40} \times 100 = 45$, so 45%.

questions.stem_md: In the same illustrative trial, a terraced plot lost only 8 tonnes of soil per hectare in a year, against 40 tonnes for up-and-down ploughing. Find the percentage reduction achieved by terracing.
questions.solution_md: Percentage $= \frac{40 - 8}{40} \times 100 = 80$, so 80%.

questions.stem_md: A farmer has 6 hectares on a slope. Ploughed up and down, the land loses 40 tonnes of soil per hectare a year (illustrative). If she terraces the whole farm and the loss falls to 8 tonnes per hectare, how many tonnes of soil does she save each year?
questions.solution_md: Saving $= 6 \times (40 - 8) = 6 \times 32 = 192$ t a year.

questions.stem_md: On an illustrative farm near Barmer, the wind speed is 30 km/h in the open and 18 km/h just behind a shelter belt. By what percentage does the shelter belt reduce the wind speed?
questions.solution_md: Percentage $= \frac{30 - 18}{30} \times 100 = 40$, so 40%.

questions.stem_md: Study the illustrative trial (soil lost in tonnes per hectare per year): ploughing up and down the slope 40; contour ploughing 22; contour ploughing with strip cropping 14; terraced field 8. (a) How many more tonnes per hectare does contour ploughing alone lose than contour ploughing with strip cropping? (b) Express this difference as a percentage of the loss under contour ploughing alone (one decimal place). (c) Why does adding grass strips reduce the loss further?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $22 - 14 = 8$ t per hectare. (b) $\frac{8}{22} \times 100 = 36.4$, about 36.4%. (c) The grass strips break the flow of water between the crop strips, trap soil washed from the strip above and protect the ground with a permanent cover.

questions.solution_md: 8 t; 36.4%; strips slow water and trap soil.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name two states where black soil is widespread and the rock from which it has formed. [2]

(b) State two differences between khadar and bhangar. [2]

(c) Explain three reasons why black soil is well suited to growing cotton. [3]

(d) Name two crops of alluvial soil, and state how the texture of alluvial soil changes from the Himalayan foothills to the delta of the Ganga. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Maharashtra and Gujarat (also Madhya Pradesh); it has formed from the weathering of basalt, the lava rock of the Deccan trap.

(b) Khadar is new alluvium on low floodplains, renewed by floods almost every year; bhangar is old alluvium on higher terraces above flood level. Khadar is more fertile; bhangar is less fertile and contains kankar.

(c) It is clayey and holds moisture for a long time, so cotton survives the dry weeks after the monsoon; it is rich in lime, potash and magnesia; deep cracks in the dry season let air in and turn the soil over (self-ploughing).

(d) Wheat and rice (also sugarcane, jute). Near the foothills it is coarse and pebbly because rivers drop heavy material as they slow down; downstream it becomes finer, and in the delta it is fine silt and clay.

questions.solution_md: Black soil states and basalt; khadar–bhangar; cotton reasons; crops and texture.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What gives red soil its colour, and why may it look yellow in places? [2]

(b) Name two states where laterite soil is found and two crops grown on it. [2]

(c) Explain how laterite soil is formed. [3]

(d) Laterite is an infertile soil, yet tea, coffee and rubber plantations flourish on laterite slopes in Kerala and Karnataka. Explain why. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Iron oxide spread through the soil makes it red; where the oxide is hydrated, in moist places, it looks yellow.

(b) Kerala and Karnataka (also Goa, Odisha, Meghalaya); cashew and tea (also coffee, rubber, coconut).

(c) It forms under high temperature and heavy rain with alternate wet and dry seasons. Rainwater percolating through the soil leaches away lime, silica and soluble nutrients. Oxides of iron and aluminium remain, giving a coarse, acidic soil that hardens in air.

(d) Plantation crops need heavy rain and warm temperatures, which these slopes provide; the sloping land drains well, which tea and coffee need; planters add plenty of manure and fertiliser to make up for the poor soil, and the crops tolerate acidic conditions.

questions.solution_md: Iron oxide; states and crops; leaching; climate, drainage and manuring.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define soil erosion and name two of its agents. [2]

(b) Name a region of India badly affected by (i) gully erosion and (ii) wind erosion. [2]

(c) Explain how the ravines of the Chambal valley were formed. [3]

(d) Explain how wind erodes soil in western Rajasthan, and why the problem becomes worse in years of drought. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Soil erosion is the removal of the top layer of soil by natural agents faster than new soil can form; agents include running water and wind (also waves and glaciers).

(b) (i) The Chambal valley in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh (or the Shivalik foothills). (ii) Western Rajasthan (the Thar desert region).

(c) The valley has deep, soft alluvial soil; monsoon rain falls in short, heavy bursts, so runoff is fast; natural cover was cleared and slopes overgrazed. Running water cut small channels that deepened, widened and joined into a maze of ravines.

(d) Strong, dry winds lift loose, fine particles from bare, sandy ground and carry them away, sometimes burying fields with sand. In drought years the soil is drier and looser, crops and grass fail so the ground is bare, and more soil is blown away.

questions.solution_md: Definition; regions; Chambal ravines; wind erosion and drought.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by soil conservation? Name two methods. [2]

(b) Distinguish between terrace farming and contour ploughing. [2]

(c) Explain how shelter belts protect farmland in western Rajasthan. [3]

(d) Suggest the most suitable method of soil conservation, with a reason, for: (i) steep slopes of the Darjeeling hills, (ii) gullies near Morena in the Chambal valley, (iii) a bare, eroded wasteland on the Shivalik slopes. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Protecting soil from erosion and maintaining its fertility; for example, terrace farming and shelter belts (also contour ploughing, afforestation).

(b) Terrace farming cuts a steep slope into flat steps, each holding water and soil; contour ploughing makes furrows across a gentle slope along lines of equal height, so each furrow slows the runoff.

(c) Rows of trees and shrubs planted across the path of the prevailing wind slow it down near the ground; they trap blowing sand before it reaches the fields; their roots bind the soil and their shade reduces drying, so less soil is lifted.

(d) (i) Terrace farming: the slopes are steep, and terraces stop water rushing down. (ii) Plugging the gullies with check dams and planting grass and trees in them: this stops the channels growing. (iii) Afforestation: tree roots bind the soil and leaf litter rebuilds humus.

questions.solution_md: Meaning; terrace versus contour; shelter belts; methods for three places.

questions.stem_md:
Study the illustrative field trial (soil lost in tonnes per hectare per year): ploughing up and down the slope 40; contour ploughing 22; contour ploughing with strip cropping 14; terraced field 8.

(a) Which method gives the least soil loss, and how many tonnes per hectare less does it lose than ploughing up and down? [2]

(b) Calculate the total soil lost in a year from a 5-hectare field under contour ploughing alone. [2]

(c) Explain why the terraced plot loses the least soil. [3]

(d) A farmer on a gentle slope in Jharkhand cannot afford to build terraces. Using the data, advise him on two methods he could use, and explain how each helps. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The terraced field; $40 - 8 = 32$ t per hectare less.

(b) $5 \times 22 = 110$ t a year.

(c) Terraces turn the slope into level steps, so water stands on each step instead of running downhill; it soaks in rather than carrying soil away; the walls or banks of each step trap any soil that moves.

(d) Contour ploughing, which cuts the loss from 40 to 22 t per hectare: furrows across the slope hold back water. Adding grass strips between crop strips (strip cropping) cuts it further to 14 t: the strips slow the water and trap soil.

questions.solution_md: Terraces, 32 t less; 110 t; level steps hold water; contour ploughing and strip cropping.
